# Graphics

Layer registry hash: `7d81999f088082653cb71ad2bd214a50ea772ac8d541fb29b51b580c15538dbb`

## The names

`framebuffer` meant five things in this tree: the UEFI boot surface in `bootproto`, the virtio-gpu
resource's DMA backing, the DisplayService scanout, an application's surface, and `pix::Target`. A
word that means five things is a word every conversation has to disambiguate and every interface
eventually gets wrong - and the way it gets wrong is that somebody passes one of the five where
another was meant, which type-checks whenever both are a pointer and a length.

Each has its own name. Nothing else in this tree is called a framebuffer.

| name | what it is | owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **FRAMEBUFFER** | the LEGACY LINEAR BOOT SURFACE and nothing else: what firmware hands over, described by `bootproto::Framebuffer` as a base, a pitch and six shift/size fields | the loader, until the display driver takes the device |
| **SCANOUT** | what the display controller is SHOWING. One per connected output, and its format is the controller's rather than an application's choice | the display driver |
| **IMAGE** | any 2D region of pixels with a layout and a meaning. A glyph mask, a decoded photograph, a filter intermediate and a depth buffer are all images | whoever allocated it |
| **SURFACE** | a PRESENTABLE application object: an image plus the presentation state that makes it something a compositor can show | the application, with DisplayService holding the presentation half |
| **RENDER TARGET** | an image a renderer is drawing INTO. A surface's image becomes one while a frame is being drawn and stops being one when it is presented | the renderer, for the duration of a frame |

## The stack

Nothing below depends on anything above it. The edges are an enumeration rather than a diagram,
because a diagram is checked by whoever reads it and a list of edges is checked by a fixture - which
is what stops a layer growing a dependency nobody agreed to, the one failure that turns a stack into
a knot.

```text
    application / UI toolkit / game / CAD / editor
         |                                    |
         |                                 scene3d
         |                                    |
      render2d                            render3d
         |                                    |
      soft2d ... future gpu2d           soft3d ... future gpu3d
         |                                    |
         +------------ graphics-core ---------+
                            |
                   Surface / present queue
                            |
                      DisplayService
                            |
                      display driver
```

| above | below | what crosses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `application` | `render2d` | a `DrawList`: paths, paints, clips, layers, filters and glyph runs |
| `application` | `scene3d` | a retained hierarchy: cameras, lights, materials, culling and animation |
| `scene3d` | `render3d` | a pass graph and the resources it names |
| `render2d` | `soft2d` | the backend interface: `prepare` then `render` |
| `render3d` | `soft3d` | the same, for three dimensions |
| `soft2d` | `graphics-core` | images, colour, sampling and compositing |
| `soft3d` | `graphics-core` | the same |
| `graphics-core` | `surface` | a presentable image and its present queue |
| `surface` | `DisplayService` | presentation: what is shown, when, and with what damage |
| `DisplayService` | `display driver` | the device transport: scanout configuration and the pages it reads |

## How somebody else's API reaches this stack

Frozen before any of them exists, because a provisional `gl*` or `vk*` API introduced to draw a demo
is the API the tree then has. Naming the routes first is what makes "properly later" a plan rather
than a hope.

| API | through | and NOT |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenGL and OpenGL ES | EGL, onto a Mesa state tracker over this stack's own surfaces | a hand-written GL front end in this tree: a second implementation of a thirty-year-old specification is not something this project can keep correct |
| Vulkan | the Khronos loader and an ICD, with Venus the likely transport to a host | a common GL/Vulkan command language invented here, which would be a third API that neither upstream tests |
| presentation | DisplayService, which owns the WSI and the present queue | an application reaching a scanout directly |
| the device | the display driver, which owns the transport | virtqueue descriptors exposed to applications, at any layer |

## Where untrusted input is validated

The point of naming a boundary is that the layer below may then ASSUME. A stack where every layer
re-checks is a stack where the check that matters is the one nobody wrote because everybody assumed
somebody else had; a stack where none does is the other failure. Each row is a place where the check
happens, and a statement that it does not happen again deeper.

| boundary | what arrives untrusted | what is checked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the loader, over firmware's hand-off | the framebuffer base, pitch, and the six shift and size fields of a `PIXEL_BIT_MASK` mode | contiguous, disjoint channel masks whose ELEMENT SIZE comes from the masks rather than from an assumed thirty-two bits |
| the image view constructor | a caller's extent, pitch, format and byte slice | a known format, a non-zero extent, a pitch at least the minimum row, and a slice at least the minimum visible bytes - all in checked arithmetic |
| `render2d`'s draw-list builder | an application's paths, paints, clips, filter graphs and resource indices | every resource index against the list's own table, every count against the profile's ceilings, and every recursive structure against its depth bound |
| the backend's `prepare` | a draw list that was built elsewhere and may have crossed a process boundary | the resource table again, because a list that arrived over a channel is not the list this process built - and the scratch it will need, which is refused up front rather than halfway through a filter chain |
| DisplayService, over a client's surface | a surface configuration, a damage region and a presented image's identity | the configuration against the output's own modes, damage against the surface extent, and the image against what the client actually owns |
| the display driver, over a device's replies | everything the device writes back, including lengths and resource identifiers it echoes | every length against the buffer it was given and every identifier against what this driver issued; a device is not trusted merely because it is a device |

The image model, the colour model, the formats and every numeric rule they need are in
[`graphics/IMAGE_COLOR_PROFILE_1.md`](graphics/IMAGE_COLOR_PROFILE_1.md).

### How a profile is hashed

| question | answer |
| --- | --- |
| the input inventory | every registry the profile is made of, in a FIXED order written in the generator - not in the order a directory listing or a hash map produces, which differ between runs and between machines |
| within a registry | the DECLARATION ORDER of the list, which is part of the profile: several of these lists are ordered on purpose - the clip planes, the render queues, the light accumulation - and sorting them would destroy the meaning the order carries |
| the text encoding | UTF-8, with LF line endings and exactly one trailing newline per line. A CRLF anywhere would make the same profile hash differently on a machine that checked out with translation |
| string encoding | verbatim, with no trimming, case folding or whitespace collapsing. A string in a registry is a value, and normalising it would make two different answers hash the same |
| integer encoding | decimal, no separators, no leading zeros, with a leading `-` for a negative value |
| float encoding | a fixed number of decimal places per field, chosen so the value round-trips - four places for a sample position, twelve for an epsilon. Never the shortest representation, which changes when a compiler's formatter changes |
| boolean encoding | `true` and `false`, which is what a reader of the canonical file sees rather than 1 and 0 |
| the hash field | EXCLUDED from its own input. The canonical form contains no hash, so the hash is a function of the profile alone and a document that states it cannot change it |
| what the document contributes | NOTHING. The Markdown is generated FROM the canonical form and is not an input to it, so a prose rewrap or a corrected example is not a profile change |
| when the hash may change | when the semantic input changes, and then the profile's VERSION changes with it. A semantic correction is a version change; a non-normative correction is neither |
| what the gate checks | that each document states the hash its registry produces, that the manifest names the same hash, and that no generated coverage table claims a feature the profile does not have |
